lead: Ray optics says whether light is trapped. It cannot say how many distinct light patterns a guide carries or how much of each pattern spills into the cladding. Maxwell's equations answer both. In a planar guide, a flat high-index layer between lower-index layers, the field can only take a few fixed shapes called modes, each travelling along the guide without changing shape. The planar guide is the simplest case to solve, and it is the base of every chip waveguide, splitter and modulator arm.
prereq: You need: total internal reflection from Ray theory: total internal reflection, acceptance angle.

sections.h3: The wave equation in a three-layer slab

blocks.text: A symmetric planar guide is a core layer of index n₁ and thickness d between two claddings of index n₂, with n₁ > n₂. The layers are wide in y, so nothing changes along y. Light travels along z, and everything we solve for varies across x, the thickness direction, with the core from x = −d/2 to x = +d/2.

In each layer Maxwell's equations reduce to the wave equation. For a wave of angular frequency ω travelling along z, write the field as E(x) ej(ωt − βz), where β is the propagation constant in rad/m. The wave equation becomes:

blocks.where: k₀ = 2π/λ is the free-space wavenumber (λ the vacuum wavelength) and n is n₁ in the core and n₂ in the cladding.

blocks.text: At x = ±d/2 the tangential components of E and H must be continuous. A guided mode oscillates in the core and decays in the cladding, which needs k₀n₂ < β < k₀n₁. Then:

items: In the core, E varies as cos(κx) or sin(κx), with transverse wavenumber κ = √(k₀²n₁² − β²).
In the cladding, E decays as e<sup>−γ(|x| − d/2)</sup>, scaled to match the core field at the wall, with decay constant γ = √(β² − k₀²n₂²).
Matching the field and its slope at the wall gives the eigenvalue equations tan(κd/2) = γ/κ for the even (cosine) modes and −cot(κd/2) = γ/κ for the odd (sine) modes.

blocks.text: These equations have only a few roots, so only a few values of β are allowed. Each root is a mode: a fixed transverse field pattern that keeps its shape as it travels. The effective index neff = β/k₀ of a mode always lies between n₂ and n₁.

sections.h3: TE and TM modes, mode number and the V number

blocks.text: Two families exist. A TE mode (transverse electric) has its electric field only along y; a TM mode (transverse magnetic) has its magnetic field only along y. Each family has its own set of β values from the same kind of matching, and in a weakly guiding slab the two sets are nearly equal.

The mode number m counts the zeros of the field across the core. TE₀ has a single central peak and no zero; TE₁ has one zero at the centre; higher m means more zeros, a smaller β and a longer evanescent tail. In ray language, a higher mode is a ray zig-zagging at a steeper angle.
One number collects thickness, wavelength and index step:

blocks.where: V is the normalized frequency (dimensionless); d is the full core thickness; λ is the vacuum wavelength in the same unit as d; √(n₁² − n₂²) is the NA of the index step.

blocks.text: With this V, mode m is guided when V > mπ, so a symmetric guide carries floor(V/π) + 1 modes of each family, and it is single-mode when V < π. TE₀ has no cutoff: a symmetric slab always guides at least one mode. Some books use the half-thickness d/2 in V; their V is half of this one and their cutoffs are V = mπ/2. Check which form a question uses.
The fraction of a mode's power inside the core is its confinement factor Γ. Near cutoff Γ is small and most of the power travels in the cladding; well above cutoff Γ approaches 1.

sections.h3: From the slab to chips and fibers

blocks.text: The planar guide is the base of integrated optics. Etching the slab into a strip adds confinement in the second direction, the subject of Integrated optical waveguides: strip and channel. Splitters, directional couplers and Mach–Zehnder modulator arms are all built from such guides.

A round fiber is the same problem in cylindrical coordinates. The fields become Bessel functions, the modes are labelled LPlm, and the fiber's V uses the core radius a: V = (2πa/λ)√(n₁² − n₂²). Its single-mode limit is V < 2.405, treated in Single-mode and multimode fibers; cutoff wavelength. The slab rule V < π does not carry over to fibers.

examples.question: A symmetric planar guide has n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.48 and core thickness d = 5 µm, used at λ = 1.3 µm. (a) Find V and the number of TE modes. (b) The eigenvalue equations, solved numerically, give effective indices 1.4969 for TE₀ and 1.4882 for TE₁. Check that both are guided, and find the decay length 1/γ of each in the cladding.
steps: Mode count: V/π = 5.90/3.142 = 1.88, so floor(1.88) + 1 = 2 TE modes (TE₀ and TE₁). TE₂ would need V > 2π = 6.28.
Guidance check: n₂ = 1.48 < 1.4882 < 1.4969 < n₁ = 1.50, so both effective indices lie in the guided range.
Check with the even-mode equation for TE₀: κ = k₀√(1.50² − 1.4969²) = 0.466 µm⁻¹, tan(κd/2) = tan(1.165) = 2.33 and γ/κ = 1.084/0.466 = 2.33. The two sides agree.
examples.answer: V = 5.90, so the guide carries two TE modes (and two TM modes). TE₀ (n<sub>eff</sub> = 1.4969) decays in the cladding over 0.92 µm; TE₁ (n<sub>eff</sub> = 1.4882) is closer to cutoff and reaches further, 1.32 µm.

traps: The slab V uses the full thickness d here, with cutoffs at mπ. If your book puts d/2 in V, the cutoffs are mπ/2. Mixing the two halves or doubles the answer.
floor(V/π) + 1 counts one family (TE). Counting TE and TM together doubles it; do not double again 'for polarization', because TE and TM already are the two polarizations.
Mode m appears when V passes mπ: TE₁ appears at V = π, not 2π. A symmetric slab with V just below π is single-mode.
A guided mode needs n₂ < n<sub>eff</sub> < n₁. A value below n₂ means the field radiates into the cladding.
A fiber uses its core radius a and the limit 2.405; a slab uses thickness d and the limit π. Do not carry one rule into the other.

quiz.q: Define a mode of a planar guide.
quiz.a: A transverse field pattern that satisfies the wave equation and the boundary conditions at both walls, oscillates in the core, decays in the cladding, and keeps its shape as it travels along z with one propagation constant β.

quiz.q: State the boundary conditions used at the core–cladding interface.
quiz.a: The tangential components of E and of H are continuous across the interface (the normal components of D and B are continuous too).

quiz.q: Why does the slab allow only discrete values of β?
quiz.a: The field must be oscillatory in the core and decaying in the cladding, and the two must match in value and slope at x = ±d/2. That matching is the transcendental condition tan(κd/2) = γ/κ (or −cot for odd modes), which has only isolated roots.

quiz.q: How do the field shape and the confinement change as the mode number m rises?
quiz.a: Each step in m adds one zero across the core, β and n<sub>eff</sub> fall towards k₀n₂, γ shrinks so the tail reaches further into the cladding, and the confinement factor drops.

quiz.q: A symmetric slab has n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.48, d = 8 µm and λ = 0.85 µm. Find V and the number of TE modes.
For n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.48 and λ = 1.3 µm, find the largest thickness that keeps the slab single-mode.
A student models a round fiber by the slab of the worked example (d = 5 µm), takes core radius 5 µm, gets V = 5.90 and reports two modes by floor(V/π) + 1. What is wrong?
quiz.a: A fiber with a 5 µm core diameter has a = 2.5 µm, so V = (2π × 2.5/1.3) × 0.2441 = 2.95. The slab count floor(V/π) + 1 does not apply to fibers: there V = 2.95 lies between 2.405 and 3.832, so the LP₀₁ and LP₁₁ groups are guided and the fiber is not single-mode.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real waveguides are not solved by hand: finite-difference and finite-element mode solvers, and the beam propagation method, give β and the field of any cross-section. Asymmetric slabs (air above, glass below) have a cutoff even for the fundamental mode, and slot waveguides squeeze light into a gap tens of nanometres wide. Search next for the slab waveguide dispersion equation, the normalized b–V diagram and finite-difference mode solvers.

figure.caption: The two TE modes of the worked example’s slab (d = 5 µm, n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.48, λ = 1.3 µm, V = 5.90), drawn from the solved eigenvalue equation. TE₀ has no zero and decays within 0.92 µm of the wall; TE₁ has one zero and, being nearer cutoff, reaches 1.32 µm into the cladding.

spec.aria: A slab with a 5 micrometre core between claddings, drawn with x vertical. Two field curves: TE0, a single hump with short tails; TE1, one positive and one negative lobe with longer tails into the cladding.
